subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Slavery and Coffee
description: A short lesson to help you apply Slavery and Coffee.

hook.text: The global coffee industry was built on forced labor. Millions of enslaved people harvested the beans.

buildup.text: Caribbean sugar plantations shifted to coffee when sugar prices fell. The enslaved workers stayed.

discovery.text: In Saint-Domingue (Haiti), coffee was the colony's second crop. The 1791 slave revolt destroyed plantations.

twist.text: After abolition, colonial powers used forced labor schemes under new names. The exploitation continued.

climax.text: Even today, labor abuses persist on some coffee farms. The supply chain's dark history echoes forward.

punchline.text: Every cup has a labor history. Not all of it is proud.

quiz.question: What happened to coffee plantations in Saint-Domingue?

details.summary: Colonial coffee production in the Americas was built on enslaved labor. Millions of enslaved Africans worked on coffee plantations in Brazil, the Caribbean, and Central America. Brazil was the last Western nation to abolish slavery in 1888, and coffee was the primary crop sustaining the system.
details.whyItMatters: Coffee's dark history of slavery cannot be separated from its story. The wealth that coffee generated was built on unimaginable human suffering.
takeaways: Colonial coffee production relied heavily on enslaved labor
Brazil used slavery in coffee until abolition in 1888
The industry's wealth was built on exploitation and suffering

faq.question: How central was slavery to coffee production?
faq.answer: In Brazil, which dominated global production, slavery was the foundation. At its peak, millions of enslaved people worked coffee plantations. The expansion of coffee and the expansion of slavery were directly linked. Even after abolition, exploitative labor conditions persisted on many plantations.

faq.question: Are there still labor abuses in coffee production today?
faq.answer: Yes. Modern labor issues include child labor, forced labor, and poverty wages in several producing countries. While not slavery, the structural exploitation of coffee workers continues. Certification programs and direct trade aim to address these issues but progress is uneven.
